body: Bernard and Thomas, 'Post-Earnings-Announcement Drift: Delayed Price Response or Risk Premium?' (Journal of Accounting Research 27, 1989; ~2,300 citations), US 1974-1986: buying the top decile of standardized unexpected earnings (SUE) and shorting the bottom decile earned about 4% abnormal over the 60 trading days after the announcement, with predictable reactions around the next quarters' announcements. Prices underreact to the fact that earnings surprises are autocorrelated. The drift was larger in small firms, and risk did not explain it. Replicated: one of the most replicated anomalies (Ball-Brown 1968 first saw it), found internationally, and it survives in HXZ in some forms. Decay: Martineau, 'Rest in Peace Post-Earnings Announcement Drift' (Critical Finance Review 2022) shows the drift in US large and mid caps has essentially vanished since about 2006 as prices react fully on the day; it survives in microcaps. Related information-flow anomalies: analyst revision momentum and earnings momentum. India: Indian quarterly results are scattered over 45 days, analyst coverage is thin below the top ~300 names, and results arrive in PDFs on exchange sites, which are all conditions for underreaction. This is untested by us. Use for us: after a genuine beat backed by cash flow and a raised order book in an under-covered Indian small cap, the move is often not over on day 1. Measure our own post-result drift on the promise-tracker names before relying on it.

data.decay: gone in US large caps post-2006 (Martineau 2022)

title: Post-earnings-announcement drift (Bernard-Thomas 1989): real, long-lived, now mostly a small-cap effect in the US
